back: A metal that contains iron. Most are magnetic and will rust unless they are protected.
A metal that contains no iron. Not magnetic and does not rust, although many tarnish or oxidise.
Iron with about 0.15–0.35% carbon. Tough, ductile, cheap and easy to weld and bend, but corrodes easily — car bodies, bicycle frames, nuts and bolts.
Iron + chromium + nickel. Shiny, hard, tough and hygienic, resisting rust and staining — cutlery, sinks, surgical instruments.
The chromium forms a thin, invisible oxide layer that re-forms if the surface is scratched.
Iron with about 0.7–1.4% carbon. Very hard and keeps a sharp edge but brittle; can be hardened and tempered — chisels, saw blades, springs.

front: Effect of adding carbon to steel
back: Harder and stronger, but more brittle and less ductile.
Very high strength-to-weight ratio, excellent corrosion resistance and biocompatible, but expensive — aircraft parts, medical implants, watch cases.
Light (low density), corrosion resistant, good conductor, malleable and easy to recycle — drinks cans, laptop casings, window frames.
Reddish-orange, excellent conductor of heat and electricity, very ductile — electrical wiring, water pipes, PCBs.
Copper + zinc. Bright gold, harder than copper, casts and machines well, low friction — door handles, taps, musical instruments.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements to improve its properties, e.g. brass, stainless steel.
The temperature at which a solid turns to a liquid. Aluminium melts at about 660°C; mild steel at about 1450°C.
Its low melting point makes it easier and cheaper to cast.
How well a material lets heat pass through it. Copper and aluminium are excellent; stainless steel is poor.
How well a material lets an electric current flow. Copper is the most widely used conductor; aluminium is used for overhead power cables.
The ability to resist being pulled apart without breaking — e.g. steel bridge cables.
The ability to absorb energy and withstand impact without breaking or cracking.
Mass per unit volume. Aluminium (about 2.7 g/cm³) is roughly a third as dense as steel (about 7.8 g/cm³).
The ability to be permanently changed in shape without cracking, keeping the new shape once the force is removed.
The ability to be hammered, pressed or rolled into shape without cracking — e.g. aluminium foil.
The ability to resist scratching, wear, cutting and indentation.
High carbon steel is hard (resists scratching) but not tough (can shatter); mild steel is tough but not especially hard.
How strong a material is compared with how heavy it is. Titanium and aluminium are high, so they are used in aircraft.
